title: Qualcomm Edges Past Estimates but Shares Fall 7% on Soft Outlook
excerpt: Adjusted earnings of $2.17 a share on $10.44 billion of revenue just beat lowered expectations, but handset sales fell 26% and the current-quarter guide came in light.
body:
• Qualcomm's fiscal Q4 2026 adjusted earnings were $2.17 per share on adjusted revenue of $10.44 billion, just ahead of the $2.16 and $10.14 billion analysts expected — but revenue was down 7% from a year earlier.
  • Handset chip sales fell 26% year over year to $5.14 billion as a global memory shortage pushes up phone prices and cuts demand.
  • Automotive revenue jumped 89% to $1.99 billion and IoT rose 4% to $1.88 billion; licensing fell 7% to $1.3 billion.
  • Guidance for the current quarter — $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion of revenue and $2.15 to $2.35 per share, against $2.27 expected — sent the shares down about 7% in extended trading.

Qualcomm edged past Wall Street's lowered expectations for its fiscal fourth quarter, then lost about 7% of its value in extended trading on a soft outlook. The chipmaker reported adjusted earnings of $2.17 per share on adjusted revenue of $10.44 billion, according to CNBC's account of the results; the LSEG consensus was $2.16 per share, and revenue consensus cited by Investing.com was $10.14 billion. A year earlier, Qualcomm had earned $3.00 per share on $11.27 billion, so adjusted revenue fell 7% year over year. On a GAAP basis, Qualcomm's release puts total revenue at $10.32 billion, down 8%, with net profit of $1.25 billion, or $1.17 per share. Amon told Reuters the current-quarter forecast includes no further sales from Apple, which is switching to its own modem chips.

Phones are the weak spot

Handset chips remain Qualcomm's largest business, and they are shrinking fast. Handset revenue fell 26% year over year to $5.14 billion, short of the $5.21 billion StreetAccount estimate, even though Qualcomm raised its own prices in September. The driver is the global memory shortage: rising memory costs are forcing handset makers to raise prices, and higher prices are cutting demand. Qualcomm said it is starting to see sequential growth in handsets and that Android shipments in China have bottomed, but it expects the overall handset market to be flat in 2027.

Cars and connected devices carry the growth

The diversification lines did the heavy lifting. Automotive revenue jumped 89% to $1.99 billion, well ahead of the $1.66 billion StreetAccount estimate. Internet of Things revenue rose 4% to $1.88 billion. Licensing (QTL) fell 7% to $1.3 billion, in line with expectations, after Qualcomm renewed agreements with Apple, Huawei and Transsion during the quarter. Total chip-division (QCT) revenue was $9.02 billion, down 8% year over year. Qualcomm also announced on Wednesday that SpaceX has selected its Dragonwing infrastructure platforms for Starlink Mobile's planned nationwide terrestrial 5G network in the US, with deployment beginning in 2027.

The $5 billion data center pitch

Chief executive Cristiano Amon is asking investors to value Qualcomm increasingly as a data center company. The business is only now starting its ramp: Amon said data center revenue is expected to exceed $650 million in the December quarter, ahead of the $539 million Visible Alpha expectation, and reiterated a target of $5 billion in data center revenue for fiscal 2027, built on custom silicon and connectivity work for customers including Amazon and Meta. The Verge has reported a target of $15 billion by 2029, with data centers eventually accounting for around 30% of the business.

"We don't have a demand issue; it's a supply issue."

— Cristiano Amon, CEO, Qualcomm

What to watch

The current-quarter guide is the near-term test: revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion and earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 per share, with the $2.25 midpoint below the $2.27 analysts expected. Beyond it, the questions are whether the handset decline really flattens as memory costs bite, and whether data center revenue can ramp from the $650 million-plus expected this quarter toward the $5 billion fiscal 2027 target Amon has set. Qualcomm sits on both sides of the AI trade — the same AI demand lifting data center budgets is inflating the memory prices that are hurting its phone business.
nri_angle: Qualcomm's shift from phone chips toward automotive, IoT and AI data centers matters for India's large chip-design workforce and for smartphone prices across the diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
